analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating insured banking from securities trading, insurance, and swaps.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would re-erect the wall between traditional banking and Wall Street speculation that Congress knocked down in 1999. Insured banks could no longer affiliate with insurance companies, securities firms, or swaps dealers, and bank holding companies would be barred from proprietary trading, market-making, hedge fund and private equity ownership, and prime brokerage. Existing combinations would have five years to unwind, and executives would have to attest under penalty of perjury that their firms comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and ordinary depositors, who would no longer stand behind — through deposit insurance and the expectation of bailouts — risky trading operations at the largest banks. The bill's own findings cite the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission's conclusion that deregulation after the Glass-Steagall repeal made the system especially vulnerable in the 2008 crisis and that traders at JPMorgan Chase made risky bets using federally insured deposits [S3]. Smaller banks would also benefit from competing against giants that no longer enjoy implicit government backing [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars insured depository institutions from affiliating with, or being under common ownership with, any insurance company, securities entity, or swaps entity, and requires existing affiliations to be terminated within five years [S2].

Prohibits bank holding companies from proprietary trading, market-making, prime brokerage, holding hedge fund or private equity fund stakes, and investing in structured or synthetic products — the activities the bill's findings link to the 2008 crisis and to the JPMorgan 'London Whale' losses [S2].
Limits national banks to core banking — deposits, credit, payments — and customer-directed securities transactions, never trading for their own account [S2].

Closes the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that allowed financial holding companies to mix banking with insurance and securities, and ends the special bankruptcy safe harbors for derivatives contracts, making financial firms treat their counterparties like everyone else in bankruptcy [S2].

Adds anti-evasion teeth: regulators must order termination of structured evasions and may impose a penalty equal to 10 percent of an entity's average net profits, and executives must attest in writing under penalty of perjury that their firm is not engaging in prohibited activities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large universal bank holding companies — the JPMorgan, Citigroup, and Bank of America model — would have to divest their trading, insurance, and securities operations within five years, and their shareholders would bear the breakup costs. Customers who value one-stop financial services could lose the ability to get banking, brokerage, and insurance from a single firm, and critics argue that a bright-line separation raises costs and pushes some activity toward less-regulated shadow banks.

drawbacks.text: The dominant banks contend that separating commercial and investment banking raises costs for consumers by ending one-stop financial services and eliminating diversification benefits, and that the Dodd-Frank Act's Volcker rule already restricts proprietary trading.

A five-year forced unwinding of conglomerate structures would be a significant operational and market transition, and the bill's own structure acknowledges compliance difficulty by providing for agency extensions of up to a year with public notice that the firm failed to comply [S3].

Activity forced out of regulated banks can migrate to less-supervised shadow-banking channels — the very dynamic the bill's cited crisis reports describe — unless supervision follows the business [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but lopsided toward the bill: it trades modest convenience losses for a small number of banking customers against removing implicit taxpayer guarantees from high-risk trading at systemically important banks. The honest caveat is that a bright-line statute can be gamed, which is why the bill pairs the prohibition with an anti-evasion clause, mandatory enforcement actions, and annual public reporting of evasion by name [S3] — but whether regulators would actually enforce it is the same open question that followed earlier banking statutes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2015 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on July 7, 2015 by Sen. Elizabeth Warren together with Sens. McCain, King, and Cantwell — a rare bipartisan, cross-ideological sponsor group — and read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S3].
It drew 9 cosponsors: 6 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 2 independents [S4].
No further action ever occurred: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal banks came out ahead: because the bill never moved, they kept the mixed banking-securities-insurance structure the bill would have unwound, along with the scale and implicit government backing that structure provides. Their shareholders faced no divestitures, and the conflict-of-interest concerns the bill cited remain unaddressed by this route.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. John McCain, Angus King, and Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction with a Republican, an independent, and a Democrat, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Richard Shelby, R-AL)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill; it received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Large Wall Street banks and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating the Glass-Steagall separation, which would have forced them to divest major business lines

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 6 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 2 independents among 9 cosponsors — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call ever showed where each party stood [S4].

industries.industry: Universal bank holding companies (JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to unwind their trading, insurance, and securities affiliates within five years and stripped the Gramm-Leach-Bliley powers their conglomerate model rests on. Their access to deposit insurance and implicit too-big-to-fail backing while running securities businesses is the taxpayer subsidy the bill was written to end, so their interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Securities underwriting, market-making, and prime brokerage desks
industries.note: Banks would be barred from underwriting issues, dealing for their own account, and prime brokerage, shrinking the client base for these businesses to standalone firms. Their profits in the current structure come partly from activities subsidized by government-insured deposits.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: Bank holding companies could no longer own, sponsor, or invest in them, cutting off a major capital source. The bill's findings describe bank-run funds as vehicles for proprietary risk-taking backed by insured deposits.
Affiliations between insured banks and insurers would be prohibited and existing ties terminated, ending the bundling of insurance with banking products.

Competing against giants whose trading operations ride on deposit insurance and bailout expectations puts them at a disadvantage; separating those operations levels the field and returns banks to their core lending role.
